decision.case_name: R (Ayinde) v London Borough of Haringey; Al-Haroun v Qatar National Bank QPSC
decision.court: High Court of Justice of England and Wales, King's Bench Division, Divisional Court (Dame Victoria Sharp P and Johnson J)
decision.retrieved_from: Courts and Tribunals Judiciary (judiciary.uk) published approved judgment PDF; judiciary.uk robots.txt permits automated access
decision.ai_tool_found: In Al-Haroun the client stated the citations were generated using publicly available AI tools, legal search engines and online sources. In Ayinde, counsel denied deliberate AI use; the court found the grounds bore the hallmarks of AI-generated text (Americanised spelling, formulaic prose).
decision.scale_note: In Al-Haroun the court's judicial assistant prepared a schedule of forty-five citations put before the court, of which eighteen were to cases that do not exist. That schedule is not reproduced in the judgment, so only the aggregate finding is recorded here.

offending.as_cited: R (on the application of El Gendi) v Camden LBC [2020] EWHC 2435 (Admin)
offending.quoted_text: the High Court emphasized that failing to provide interim accommodation during the review process undermines the protective purpose of the homelessness legislation. The court found that such a failure not only constitutes a breach of statutory duty but also creates unnecessary hardship for vulnerable individuals.
offending.filing: Grounds for judicial review settled by Ms Sarah Forey, R (Ayinde) v Haringey
offending.court_quote: The case that is cited (El Gendi) does not exist. There is no case with that name, held by the National Archives, or anywhere else. The neutral citation number, [2020] EWHC 2435 (Admin), does exist, but it is the citation reference to a different case: R (Preservation and Promotion of the Arts Ltd) v Greater Manchester Magistrates' Court [2020] EWHC 2435 (Admin). That case concerns a charity's liability to pay business rates. It has nothing to do with duties under the Housing Act 1996.
offending.what_actually_exists: The neutral citation [2020] EWHC 2435 (Admin) belongs to R (Preservation and Promotion of the Arts Ltd) v Greater Manchester Magistrates' Court, a case about a charity's liability to pay business rates.

offending.as_cited: R (on the application of Ibrahim) v Waltham Forest LBC [2019] EWHC 1873 (Admin)
offending.quoted_text: the court quashed a local authority decision due to its failure to properly consider the applicant's medical needs, underscoring the necessity for careful evaluation of such evidence in homelessness determinations.
offending.filing: Grounds for judicial review settled by Ms Sarah Forey, R (Ayinde) v Haringey
offending.court_quote: The four further cases cited by Ms Forey do not exist either. We note too the Americanised spelling of “emphasized”, which contrasts with the English spelling of the same word by Ms Forey in correspondence; and further, the somewhat formulaic style of the prose.

offending.as_cited: R (on the application of H) v Ealing LBC [2021] EWHC 939 (Admin)
offending.quoted_text: where the court found the local authority's failure to provide interim accommodation irrational in light of the applicant's vulnerability and the potential consequences of homelessness.
offending.filing: Grounds for judicial review settled by Ms Sarah Forey, R (Ayinde) v Haringey
offending.court_quote: The four further cases cited by Ms Forey do not exist either.

offending.as_cited: R (on the application of KN) v Barnet LBC [2020] EWHC 1066 (Admin)
offending.quoted_text: where the court held that procedural fairness includes timely decision-making and the provision of necessary accommodations during the review process.
offending.filing: Grounds for judicial review settled by Ms Sarah Forey, R (Ayinde) v Haringey
offending.court_quote: The four further cases cited by Ms Forey do not exist either.

offending.as_cited: R (on the application of Balogun) v LB Lambeth [2020] EWCA Civ 1442
offending.quoted_text: where the Court of Appeal emphasized that local authorities must ensure fair treatment of applicants in the homelessness review process.
offending.filing: Grounds for judicial review settled by Ms Sarah Forey, R (Ayinde) v Haringey
offending.court_quote: The four further cases cited by Ms Forey do not exist either. We note too the Americanised spelling of “emphasized” …

offending.quoted_text: The statutory duty under Section 188(3) of the Housing Act 1996 requires a local authority to provide interim accommodation when an individual has applied for a review of a homelessness decision.
offending.filing: Grounds for judicial review settled by Ms Sarah Forey, R (Ayinde) v Haringey
offending.court_quote: This misstates the effect of section 188(3). Section 188(3) provides that: “…the authority may secure that accommodation is available for the applicant's occupation pending a decision on review.”
offending.what_actually_exists: Section 188(3) confers a power (“may secure”), not a duty, to secure accommodation pending a review decision.

offending.as_cited: [Aggregate finding] eighteen of forty-five citations put before the court in Al-Haroun v Qatar National Bank
offending.cited_case_name: multiple — schedule of forty-five citations prepared by the court's judicial assistant
offending.filing: Witness statements of Mr Hamad Al-Haroun and his solicitor Mr Abid Hussain, and related correspondence, Al-Haroun v Qatar National Bank QPSC
offending.court_quote: The schedule of references referred to by Dias J lists forty five citations that had been put before the court. In eighteen instances, the case cited does not exist. In respect of those cases that did exist, in many instances they did not contain the quotations that were attributed to them, did not support the propositions for which they were cited, and did not have any relevance to the subject matter of the application. In the judicial assistant's pithy conclusion “The vast majority of the authorities are made up or misunderstood.”
offending.what_actually_exists: Twenty-seven of the forty-five cited authorities exist, but many did not contain the quotations attributed to them, did not support the propositions cited, and were irrelevant to the subject matter.

offending.as_cited: [Aggregate finding] the real authorities among the forty-five in Al-Haroun v Qatar National Bank
offending.cited_case_name: multiple — real authorities in the same schedule
offending.filing: Witness statements of Mr Al-Haroun and Mr Hussain, Al-Haroun v Qatar National Bank QPSC
offending.court_quote: “The court is deeply troubled and concerned by the fact that in the course of correspondence with the court and in the witness statements of both Mr Al-Haroun and Mr Hussain, reliance is placed on numerous authorities, many of which appear to be either completely fictitious or which, if they exist at all, do not contain the passages supposedly quoted from them, or do not support the propositions for which they are cited …”
offending.what_actually_exists: Some of the cited authorities exist but do not contain the quoted passages or support the propositions cited.

controls.as_cited: Ex parte Lee 673 SW 3d 755 (Tex App Waco 19 July 2023)
controls.cited_for: that non-existent cases were cited to the Tenth Court of Appeals for the State of Texas, which declined to issue a show cause order
controls.court_quote: In Ex parte Lee 673 SW 3d 755 (Tex App Waco 19 July 2023) non-existent cases were cited to the Tenth Court of Appeals for the State of Texas. The court … “resist[ed] the temptation to issue a show cause order... or report the attorney to the State Bar of Texas for a potential investigation for a violation of the State Bar rules.”

controls.as_cited: Kohls v Elison No 24-cv-3754 (D Minn 10 January 2025)
controls.cited_for: that an expert on AI and misinformation used generative AI to draft a report that included citations of non-existent academic articles
controls.court_quote: “The irony. …a credentialed expert on the dangers of AI and misinformation, has fallen victim to the siren call of relying too heavily on AI – in a case that revolves around the dangers of AI, no less. … The Court thus adds its voice to a growing chorus around the country declaring the same message: verify AI-generated content in legal submissions!”
controls.what_actually_exists: The case is real and the citation resolves. Note that the judgment spells the respondent “Elison”; the United States case is Kohls v. Ellison, No. 24-cv-3754 (LMP/DLM) (D. Minn. Jan. 10, 2025). The court's spelling is preserved in as_cited because this record is a control and the string handed to a verifier must be the string the court wrote.
